newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Helicopter collision spurs Israel's Lebanon debate.
newsitem.headline: Helicopter collision spurs Israel's Lebanon debate.

text.p: Even before all 73 dead had been counted, the mid-air crash of two Lebanon-bound military helicopters was reviving debate over the cost of Israeli involvement there.

The army said guerrillas were not behind the disaster but the loss of so many soldiers, most about 20 years old and on their way to fight in Lebanon, raised questions about the value of their mission.

Israeli politicians left and right united in shock and grief, vowing to remain steadfast against the Iranian-backed Islamist guerrillas of Hizbollah -- "the Party of God" -- fighting Israel in south Lebanon.

But the stage has been set for a dispute over policy in Lebanon. The helicopters were taking the troops to a 15 km (nine-mile)-wide occupation zone that Israel carved out in Lebanon in 1985 as a buffer against guerrilla attacks.

Opposition leader Shimon Peres -- who as prime minister got stuck in what Israelis typically call "the Lebanese mud" during a 17-day blitz last April -- urged accelerating peace talks with Beirut and with Damascus, the main power broker in Lebanon.

"We cannot pull out unilaterally but we also cannot stay this way forever," said Peres, who narrowly lost an election last May in part because of Arab voters' anger at the killing of Lebanese civilians during the Israeli bombardment.
The 73 soldiers killed in Tuesday night's collision -- there were no survivors -- exceeded the 70 who died battling Hizbollah over the last three years.
"It takes Hizbollah three years to do what one malfunction did here," Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on a visit to the crash site in northern Israel on Wednesday.
"I think the jubilation we heard from Hizbollah tells you who we are dealing with. These people's goal is not to get us out of Lebanon but to get us out of Israel," he told reporters.

The army's helicopter airlift aimed to sidestep Hizbollah bombs along Lebanon's roads. Last week three Israelis died in such a blast. This week Public Security Minister Avigdor Kahalani complained soldiers had become "sitting ducks".

"There is no tool, no trick, no device that the Israel Defence Forces have not tried to reduce the losses of this war. But the war is winning," wrote columnist Nahum Barnea in the newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth on Wednesday.
"The soldiers who died in the accident last night fell in the war against Hizbollah," he wrote.

Israel's most unpopular war among its own citizens, in 1982, began when troops under hawkish Defence Minister Ariel Sharon invaded Lebanon with the avowed aim of driving back Palestinian guerrillas firing Katyusha rockets at northern Israel.
The invasion angered the Lebanese, giving rise to Hizbollah, as well as many Israelis who felt misled when their troops thrust all the way to Beirut and losses reached 650 soldiers.

The troops pulled back to the current occupation zone three years later and settled into a war of attrition with Hizbollah. A loss of nearly 200 Israeli soldiers in the 12 years since has prompted Israeli calls for a political solution.

Peace talks launched with Damascus in 1991 have been stuck over the fate of the Golan Heights that Israel seized from Syria 1967. Syrian President Hafez al-Assad demands a full Israeli pullout but Netanyahu refuses to cede any of the strategic plateau.
Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai last week demanded Beirut supress Hizbollah. Other leaders blamed Syria, which has some 30,000 troops in Lebanon, for backing Hizbollah.

Since Netanyahu broke a deadlock with Palestinians by handing over most of Hebron last month, Israeli leaders have talked of peace with Damascus. Washington is seeking a "bridging formula" to revive talks cut off by Israel nearly a year ago.

A proposal by Netanyahu to negotiate security guarantees for an Israeli withdrawal from "Lebanon First" was rejected last year by Lebanon and Syriam who called it a ploy to avoid returning the Golan. Since then Israeli tensions with the two countries have ebbed and flowed.
Some analysts and pollsters insist that ultimately Israelis would overcome their doubts and hand back the Golan in return for solid security arrangements and a softening of Syrian attitudes.

Cracks have surfaced in Israel's right wing. Four members of parliament from Netanyahu's Likud-Gesher-Tsomet bloc say they would be willing to make territorial concessions to Syria under certain conditions.
